opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the most striking thing about AlphaFold 2 is how it changed the starting point for so many scientists. Before, if you wanted the structure of a protein, you often had to spend months or even years on experimental work, with crystallography, cryo-EM, or NMR, and sometimes it simply didn't work. The structure was the end goal of a whole PhD.

What AlphaFold did was turn that into something closer to a lookup. When we released structure predictions for essentially all known proteins, around 200 million of them, through the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database with EMBL-EBI, a researcher anywhere in the world could get a high-quality hypothesis about their protein's shape in seconds. That democratization is, to me, the deepest part of the impact. It isn't just the big labs with expensive equipment. It's a scientist working on a neglected tropical disease, or someone studying plant biology or enzymes that break down plastics, who now has structural insight they never would have had.

It also changed the kinds of questions people ask. Experimental structural biologists didn't become obsolete. Their work shifted. They can use predictions to guide experiments, solve harder structures faster, and focus on what predictions still struggle with: dynamics, conformational changes, complexes, and interactions with other molecules. So the frontier moved. People went from asking "What does this protein look like?" to "How does it move, what does it bind to, and how can we design something new?"

And I think there's a broader lesson there, which we care about a lot at DeepMind. When AI solves a root-node problem, something that sits underneath many other scientific questions, the benefits cascade in ways you can't fully predict. We've seen AlphaFold cited in work across drug discovery, vaccine research, and fundamental biology that we never anticipated. That's really what you hope for with AI for science. You aren't just answering one question. You're giving the whole community a new instrument.

r001.rationale: It contrasts months or years of experimental work with getting a structural hypothesis in seconds.

r002.rationale: It says researchers anywhere can access predictions and specifically notes that scientists without expensive equipment gain structural insight.

r003.rationale: It describes using predictions to guide experiments and designing something new, and mentions drug discovery, but does not clearly explain a shift toward using structural knowledge to develop treatments.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the simplest way to put it is that AlphaFold 2 changed what counts as a bottleneck. For about fifty years, if you wanted to know the three-dimensional structure of a protein, you were looking at an experimental campaign. Crystallography, NMR, later cryo-EM. That might take a postdoc a year, sometimes an entire PhD, and sometimes it would just never work for that particular protein. So the structure itself was the scarce, expensive thing, and a lot of research programmes were shaped around which structures you could realistically get.

What AlphaFold 2 did was make a good structural hypothesis essentially free. We went from something like a couple hundred thousand experimentally determined structures to predictions for more or less the entire known protein universe, over two hundred million, available in a database anyone can query. That means the question a scientist asks on a Monday morning is different. It is no longer "can I get a structure," it is "what do I do with it." You can look at a protein you have never worked on, see where the binding pocket probably is, see how a disease mutation might sit relative to an interface, and design your experiment around that.

I want to be careful not to overclaim, though. A prediction is a hypothesis. It is a very good one for many proteins, and the model gives you a confidence estimate so you know where to trust it and where not to. But it does not tell you about dynamics, it does not by itself tell you about every complex or every disordered region, and the experimentalists are still absolutely essential. If anything, their time is now spent on harder, more interesting problems rather than on things the model can do.

The other impact, and this is the one I find most exciting as a researcher, is what it did to the field's ambition. It showed that a learned model could reach experimental accuracy on a problem that people had been chipping at for decades. Once that happens, biologists start asking what else might be tractable: protein interactions, binding to small molecules, designing new proteins from scratch, eventually modelling larger pieces of the cell. So the direct effect was democratising structure. The indirect effect was expanding what structural biologists feel they are allowed to try.

r001.rationale: The response says structural hypotheses became essentially free and contrasts predictions with year-long experimental campaigns, but it does not state that obtaining structures went from months to seconds.

r002.rationale: It says predictions for over two hundred million proteins are in a database anyone can query, calls the direct effect “democratising structure,” and contrasts this with scarce, expensive experimental determination.

r003.rationale: It describes shifting from obtaining structures to using them to guide experiments, but does not say scientists use that knowledge to develop treatments.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest impact is that it changes the questions scientists can afford to ask. Determining a protein’s structure experimentally can take a tremendous amount of time and effort. When you can get a useful structural prediction much more quickly, you have a starting point for understanding how that protein works, what might happen when it changes, and which experiments to do next.

That doesn’t mean structural biology is solved. A structure is not a complete account of a protein’s behaviour—how it moves, how it interacts with other molecules, or how it functions inside a cell. And a prediction still needs to be assessed carefully. But it can remove a major bottleneck, allowing scientists to spend more of their effort on those deeper biological questions.

So the exciting thing is not just doing existing work faster. It’s making projects feasible that previously might have been too difficult or too expensive to pursue.

r001.rationale: The response says predictions are available much more quickly, but does not state that structure determination went from months to seconds.

r002.rationale: It says predictions can make difficult or expensive projects feasible, but does not identify scientists lacking resources for experimental structure determination as the beneficiaries.

r003.rationale: It describes shifting effort toward biological questions and choosing experiments, but does not mention using structural knowledge to develop treatments.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AlphaFold 2 changes the starting point for a lot of research. Understanding a protein’s structure can help scientists reason about how it works, but obtaining that structure experimentally can take a tremendous amount of effort. Having a useful prediction means they can begin asking biological questions much sooner.

It also makes some projects feasible that might previously have been too costly or too uncertain to pursue. Researchers can use a predicted structure to form hypotheses, choose experiments, and interpret their results. The important point is that a prediction doesn’t answer every question: proteins move, interact with other molecules, and function in particular cellular environments. Experiments remain essential. But scientists now have a powerful additional tool that can help them decide where to look and what to test.

r001.rationale: The response says predictions let scientists begin biological questions sooner, but does not state that structure determination went from months to seconds.

r002.rationale: It mentions projects that were too costly may now be feasible, but does not identify scientists lacking resources for experimental structure determination as gaining access.

r003.rationale: The response describes using predictions to form hypotheses and choose experiments, but does not describe a shift toward developing treatments.
